title: Measurement
one_line_goal: Memory, CPU, timing and network logged, and the numbers proven accurate
summary: Ferrum learns to measure itself: memory, CPU, startup and page-load timing, plus a network log of addresses and timings only. Each meter is checked against helper programs with known usage; a meter that fails blocks P6. You chose: full addresses kept, log off unless switched on, logs deleted after 14 days.

tasks.title: Export file format and run labels
tasks.what: One versioned format for all result files, with a label on every run: code version, Windows build, WebView2 version, settings and machine.
tasks.why: A number that cannot be traced back to its setup is worthless for research: nobody could repeat it, and a quiet change in versions could explain any difference.
tasks.how: Write the format as files in the repo (one record per line, plus a table form) and a writer that never leaves a half-written file and starts new files in turn.
tasks.chain: Every later result is read from files → define one versioned format (plain data files) that labels each run with code version, Windows build, WebView2 version and settings → any number can be traced to the exact setup that made it.
tasks.check: Each record type saves and reloads unchanged; a checker accepts good files and rejects a damaged one.

tasks.title: Count only Ferrum's own processes
tasks.what: Finding exactly which processes belong to Ferrum.
tasks.why: Counting another app's processes would make Ferrum look heavier than it is, or hide its real use. Every later memory number depends on this.
tasks.how: Ask Ferrum's own WebView2 setup for the processes it started, add Ferrum's main process, and never pick processes by program name.
tasks.chain: Other apps on the PC also use WebView2 → find Ferrum's processes through Ferrum's own WebView2 setup, never by program name → other apps' memory never leaks into Ferrum's numbers.
tasks.check: A test runs Ferrum next to another WebView2 app: every Ferrum process is counted, none of the other app's.

tasks.title: Memory and CPU meter
tasks.what: A meter that reads the memory and CPU use of Ferrum's processes at a chosen interval.
tasks.why: Adding up memory the wrong way counts shared memory twice and makes every app look bigger. Fair totals are needed before any comparison.
tasks.how: Call Windows directly, add up across Ferrum's processes, and take peaks from that total, never by adding per-process peaks. Tests check the sums.
tasks.chain: We need trustworthy memory and CPU numbers → read them straight from Windows (private memory as the headline, working set as secondary, CPU time) and add them up over Ferrum's processes → one fair total per moment; peaks come from the total, never from adding per-process peaks.
tasks.check: Tests confirm totals and peaks are computed correctly.

tasks.title: Prove the meter is accurate
tasks.what: Proof that the meter is accurate.
tasks.why: An unchecked meter could be off by any amount, and every P6 result would carry that error without anyone knowing.
tasks.how: Helper programs use a known amount of memory and CPU. Compare the meter and an independent reader with those values, using tolerances written down before the run.
tasks.chain: A meter is only useful if it is right → helper programs use a known amount of memory and CPU; the meter and an independent reader are compared with those values, with tolerances written down before the run → a meter that fails blocks P6.
tasks.check: Readings fall within the tolerances written beforehand; raw outputs saved as evidence.

tasks.title: Measure the meter's own cost
tasks.what: Measuring the meter's own CPU and memory use at each sampling speed.
tasks.why: Measuring takes some CPU and memory itself. If that cost is unknown, part of what looks like Ferrum's use may be the meter's.
tasks.how: Run the meter at each sampling speed it supports and record the CPU time and private memory the meter itself uses.
tasks.chain: Measuring uses some CPU and memory itself → measure the meter's own cost at each sampling speed → we know how much it disturbs results (this describes the tool, not Ferrum).
tasks.check: Raw outputs saved as evidence; no comparison claims made.

tasks.title: Startup timing
tasks.what: Startup timing: process start, window visible, shell first drawn, first content drawn and largest content drawn.
tasks.why: Fast start is one of the things Ferrum is meant to be good at. Timing read by page scripts can change what is being timed, so Ferrum reads it itself.
tasks.how: Ferrum reads these moments itself through the browser's debugging channel, never through page scripts. Checked: both content moments are read this way.
tasks.chain: Startup speed is a key result → record when the process starts, the window appears, and the first and largest content are drawn, read by Ferrum itself through the browser's debugging channel → startup can be compared fairly in P6.
tasks.check: On a test page every moment is recorded, in the right order.

tasks.title: Page-load timing
tasks.what: Page-load timing: start, response, page ready, fully loaded and done, with same-site or cross-site labels and the redirect count.
tasks.why: Without the cross-site label and redirect count, a slow load could be blamed on Ferrum when the site itself sent the browser through several addresses.
tasks.how: Record these moments for every load. A test reuses the P2 redirect test pages and checks the redirect count and the order of the times.
tasks.chain: Page-load speed is another key result → record each load's main moments, whether it crossed to another site, and how many redirects it took → page loads can be compared fairly in P6.
tasks.check: Test pages with known redirects give the right redirect count and timing order.

tasks.title: Record tab state changes
tasks.what: A record format for tab state changes (from, to, why, when, which tab), logged now for hide and show.
tasks.why: If tab sleeping in P7 needed a new record format, earlier data could not be compared with later data, and the measuring code would change mid-study.
tasks.how: Add the tab-change record as one more type in the result file format, and have Ferrum write one each time a tab is hidden or shown.
tasks.chain: Smart tab sleeping in P7 needs a record of every tab state change → define the record (from, to, why, when, which tab) and log hide and show now → P7 plugs in without a new format.
tasks.check: Switching tabs produces hide and show records that pass the format check.

tasks.title: Network log: addresses and timings only
tasks.what: A network log with only address, method, result, type, timing, sizes, tab and security decision, one folder per session.
tasks.why: Headers and page content can hold passwords and personal data. A log that stored them would be a privacy risk on your computer.
tasks.how: Use WebView2's response event per tab, or the debugging channel if an earlier test showed problems. A test proves no headers or content are stored.
tasks.chain: You asked for a log of network calls → per tab, save address, method, result, type, timing, size and the security decision to one folder per session, never headers or page content → useful for research without storing private data.
tasks.check: A test page with known requests gives exactly the expected entries; a test proves no headers or content are stored.

tasks.title: Network log: coverage and cost
tasks.what: A check of which requests the network log catches, plus a small trial of its cost.
tasks.why: If the log quietly misses some requests, a paper that relies on it would draw wrong conclusions. Stating its gaps keeps the claims honest.
tasks.how: Test embedded frames, redirects and background-worker requests and mark each covered or not. Checked: frames and requests a worker passes on are reported; a worker's own requests are not. Save the trial output.
tasks.chain: Some requests may be missed (embedded frames, redirects, background workers) → test each kind and run a small cost trial → the paper states exactly what the log covers.
tasks.check: A coverage table and the cost-trial output are saved as evidence.

tasks.title: Settings for measuring and logging
tasks.what: Settings to turn measuring and the network log on or off, open the log folder, and set how long logs are kept.
tasks.why: Measuring and logging write data about your browsing. Without switches you could not stop it, and old logs would pile up.
tasks.how: Add on/off switches, a retention limit and an 'open log folder' button to the settings, and have the meter and the network log check their switch before writing.
tasks.chain: You decide what is recorded → add on/off switches for measurement and the network log, a button to open the log folder, and a retention limit → nothing is recorded that you did not choose.
tasks.check: A quick test flips each switch and confirms files are or are not written.

tasks.title: Map tabs to browser processes
tasks.what: A follow-up check of how several tabs show up in the debugging channel and which browser processes serve which tab.
tasks.why: If several tabs share one process, a number given 'per tab' may really belong to several. Treating it as one tab's use would mislead P6 and P7.
tasks.how: Open several tabs in Ferrum, list how each one appears in the debugging channel, and match the browser processes to the tabs they serve.
tasks.chain: Tabs may share browser processes → check how each tab shows up and which processes serve it → P6 and P7 know how far per-tab numbers can be trusted.
tasks.check: Findings saved as evidence; each open assumption confirmed or moved to a later phase.

tasks.title: Reading: measurement methods
tasks.what: A batch of reading on measurement methods and browser benchmarking practice.
tasks.why: Measurement definitions that ignore common practice would make Ferrum's numbers hard to compare with other studies, and reviewers would question them.
tasks.how: Read the literature on measurement and browser benchmarking, write dated notes, and use them with the accuracy results to fix each headline measurement's definition.
tasks.chain: Our methods must match good practice → read the literature on measurement and browser benchmarking → each headline measurement gets a final, cited definition.
tasks.check: New research notes saved; each headline measurement is marked defined and cites the accuracy test.

tasks.title: Stop requests to blocked sites
tasks.what: Ferrum stops requests to a blocked site at the network level, not only its page: typed addresses, links, redirects, frames, images and scripts.
tasks.why: Today a blocked site's page is hidden, but the site still receives the request and can see that someone asked for it.
tasks.how: Filter the requests themselves with WebView2's request event and refuse those to blocked sites; test every way in against the test server's request counter.
tasks.chain: A blocked site still receives the request → stop it at the network level for every way in → a blocked site really gets nothing.
tasks.check: The test server counts no request for a blocked site after every kind of attempt; allowed sites still load; the cost is measured.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.what: The phase gate and your review.
tasks.why: P6 builds every comparison on this meter and this log. If either is wrong or leaks private data, all later results are affected.
tasks.how: The gate script runs every check and saves evidence. You browse with the network log on, check the log folder for anything private, test the switches and approve.
tasks.chain: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the accuracy results and the privacy check and approve; only then does P6 start.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist, the wiki check is clean, and you approve the end of P5.

test_gate.explanation: Code and tests pass → the meters match known values → exported files match the format → the network log holds no private data → earlier features still work → you browse with logging on and check the log folder → you approve. Only then does P6 start.

rows.proves: Code is tidy and warning-free, all automatic tests pass, and the release build works.
Third-party libraries have acceptable licences and no known security problems.
Memory and CPU readings match known values within the written tolerances.
Exported files match the published format.
Exactly the expected requests are logged, with no headers or content.
Security, tabs and basic browsing tests still pass.
The plan pages are consistent and have no broken links.
You browse for a session with logging on and find nothing in the log that should not be there.
The on/off switches behave as described.
